questions.stem: Prove by mathematical induction that 1³ + 2³ + 3³ + … + n³ = n²(n + 1)²/4.
questions.notes: STAR GUTTER CLIPPED on printed p.25 — the scan loses about one character at the left edge (Sol: prints as ol:). Recorded 0 is a FLOOR, not a reading. Each sub-part reprints the instruction Prove by mathematical induction, so the two are separate questions.

questions.stem: Prove by mathematical induction that 1² + 2² + 3² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.
questions.notes: Star gutter clipped on printed p.25. Recorded 0 is a floor.

questions.stem: Prove by mathematical induction that a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) + … up to n terms = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d].
Prove by induction that a + ar + ar² + … up to n terms = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), r ≠ 1.

questions.notes: The stars sit on the SUB-PARTS here, not on the number. The number 5. itself is lost in the clipped left gutter of printed p.27; it is fixed by the tail of printed p.26, which shows 5.*** in its right margin.

questions.stem: Show that 1² + (1² + 2²) + (1² + 2² + 3²) + … up to n terms = n(n + 1)²(n + 2)/12, ∀ n ∈ N.
Show that 49ⁿ + 16n − 1 is divisible by 64, ∀ n ∈ N.
questions.notes: The number 7 carries no stars of its own; each sub-part carries its own count. Q7 opens on printed p.28 and its parts ii) and iii) run onto p.29.

questions.stem: If x and y are natural numbers with x ≠ y, show by mathematical induction that xⁿ − yⁿ is divisible by x − y, ∀ n ∈ N.
Use mathematical induction to prove that 2 + 3·2 + 4·2² + … up to n terms = n·2ⁿ, ∀ n ∈ N.
Use mathematical induction to prove that 4³ + 8³ + 12³ + … up to n terms = 16n²(n + 1)².
